Following up the state ment made by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), I may say that I have already brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of the Interior, and I believe the facts stated in the article referred to to be substantially correct as I nave received a letter from home confirming them. Such representations should be made to the government of the United States that conduct of this kind on the part of their officials will not be repeated. It seems to me that both Canadian and American officials engaged in the enforcement of immigration Acts should be taught that one of their first duties is to dispense courtesy and kindness rather than heckling, browbeating and humiliation to the parties with whom they have to deal, and in this particular case they should be severely censured for the conduct of which they have been guilty. I know the fajpily that has been mentioned very well and they are one of the most respectable families in my county.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In order that there may be no misapprehension as to the responsibility attached to the conduct of this government, I would like to emphasize the fact to the House that the action is taken by the United States officers and is taken in respect of people who, if not already citizens of the United States, propose to become citizens of that country. Their conduct is not such as this government is responsble for except indirectly. Perhaps it may be well for me to explain to the House just how far that responsibility extends in the case which has arisen. Under the immigration exclusion laws of the United States, as under the immigrant exclusion laws of Canada, provision is made for the exclusion at the border of people who are deemed undesirable by the immigration officials of either country. In order that there may be an efficient examination of people who are crossing at the border, and in order that railway traffic may not be delayed, it has been the custom of the United States officers to board trains destined for the United States, in Canada, for the purpose of making their examination of passengers on the train before they reach the border, so that there will be no delay at the border. The alternative of that arrangement would be that trains arriving at the border would be held there the same as they are for customs purposes, until the examination was made. Of course that would involve a very serious delay to railway traffic. So the immigration officers of the United States do the same as the customs officers of the United States, that is, for the convenience of travellers, they board trains in Canada and make the examination on Mr ARMSTRONG.
the train, so that the examination may be as far as possible completed by the time the train arrives at the frontier.
Do Canadian officers board American trains in the same way?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In some cases where it is considered necessary. But I may remark that the exclusion arrangements of the United States are much more elaborate and extensive, and involve the employment of a much larger staff, than do the exclusion arrangements of Canada. Therefore the United States employ a much larger number of men than Canada is able to em-plov, or needs to employ. We run our exclusion business on a much cheaper scale than the United States, although we think it is equally efficient. Now in the handling of the exclusion act along 3,000 miles of the frontier, and where so large number of men are employed, doubtless it frequently happens that some of these men are not all they ought to be for the purpose for which they are employed, and sometimes they make mistakes, sometimes they inflict hardships needlessly. I would like to say, however, that so far as our experience has gone in dealing with the United States officers engaged on the immigration service, when we have brought to their attention any case of hardship or impropriety on the part of United States officials, we have received very fair consideration at the hands of the head of the immigration service of that country. We have never failed to bring such instances to their attention, and so far they have never failed in giving us reasonable satisfaction

Before the orders of the day are called, I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Public Works to a couple of articles which have appeared in the Chatham local papers protesting against the provincial authorities removing a large portion of the forest on Rondeau park. One of those articles states that the provincial government is going right ahead and is destroying the natural forest which protects the Rondeau harbour. That is the statement of a Mr. Watson, who is a prominent lumberman of that particular district, and is well acquainted with the locality, and knows how important this forest is to the Rondeau harbour on which the Dominion government are spending three hundred thousand dollars to make it the best harbour on Lake Erie. The action of this government in this respect has met with the general approval of people in the western part of Ontario. They regret to see this forest, which consists of hundreds of acres, damaged to such an extent that by the removal of large trees the smaller

ones are likely to be overthrown by the heavy storms that occur in the fall of the year. I think that if the Minister of Public Works will take up this matter with the Minister of Lands and Mines of the provincial government, the latter gentleman may be induced to cease operations, and I know that such action on the part of this government would meet with general approval, because there is a very widespread protest about the removal of these trees. I think that last fall when some of the leading Toronto papers took the matter up, it was generally understood that the work would be stopped, at least for a while. I hope that the minister will take the matter up with the provincial authorities, and see if measures cannot be taken to protect that harbour, and prevent the destruction of the timber which beautifies that part of the country.

The matter to which my hon. friend has called attention is one of a good deal of importance. But he will realize that the only ground upon wdiich this government could intervene would be that the cutting away of the forest is likely to be injurious to the harbour and injurious to navigation. I can understand that under certain circumstances that might be the case; whether it is the case at Rondeau I am not at present prepared to say. However, the matter is of a good deal of importance, and I should be glad to communicate with the proper minister of the provincial government in regard to it. I shall be very glad indeed if the views my hon. friend has presented can be met.

I desire to call the attention of the Minister of the Interior to what appears to be a very serious grievance in connection with the exclusion of immigrants. There is a requirement that immigrants entering Canada shall each be possessed of a certain sum of money, and I have information to-day as to a case in Toronto in this connection which is one of great hardship. These immigrants are most of them illiterate and unable to speak the English language, so that they are not aware of what qualifications will be required of them ivhen they arrive at a Canadian port. If they have not the required amount of money pei capita they are then deported. A change has recently been made in the regulations in this respect, as heretofore each immigrant was not required to be in possession of a sum of money. I submit that the government should take precaution to inform those immigrants on the other side what qualifications will be required of them, and not have them come to a Canadian port under a misapprehension and
be subject to the harsh treatment of deportation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This question lies at the very root of the subject of immigration. It is a question as to whether we are to exercise a selective and restrictive policy or not. I take it that the will of parliament is, as expressed in the Immigration Act, that we should exercise a selective and restrictive policy in regard to immigration, and the government must carry out the will of parliament which cannot be done without occasional cases of hardship. Let the members of this House thoroughly understand that in giving sanction to restrictive and selective laws they assume responsibility on behalf of themselves and their constituents for the hardships that necessarily arise in the adminstration of these laws. It is not possible that every person in every part of the world who makes up his mind to come to Canada shall be previously informed by the government of Canada as to the regulations. All that can be done is that the government -shall do what is reasonably possible to give due notice to the world as to wdiat the requirements, are. In 1908 an order in council was passed requiring that each immigrant should have a stated sum of money in order that he might be admitted into Canada. The first order in _ council passed required the money qualification to cover a certain term, and when that term expired another order in council was passed continuing the money qualification until the order should be repealed. These orders Were, of course, passed under the authority of the Immigration, Act. It is, therefore, more than two years since notice was given as to a money qualification being required. In view of the difficulty that people generally might not be conversant with the letter of the law', at the close of the last immigration season, on the 4th of June, 1909, a departmental circular wras issued which gave notice to every one it could reach as to the policy of and the administration of the Department of the Interior in regard to the selection of immigrants. On June the 4th, 1909, this circular was sent to the steamship companies, to booking agents, to anybody we knew of who wras interested in immigration, and the steamship companies reprinted the circular and published it in Europe as a part-of their information to immigrants. This circular set out that each immigrant was required to have $25 in cash on his arrival -in Canada except he wras going to farm work or going to certain specified relatives who were able and willing to support him. The shipping companies reprinted that circular and it was circulated through Europe bv them. I submit to the House and to the country that the Immigration Department has done all that

reasonably can be expected of it to give notice to the world as to what our regulations and requirements would be. The assertion that there has been any change in these regulations in regard to the amount of money required is not correct. It was found after administering the immigration law for nearly a year under the circular issued, that the circular was not in all particulars supported by the law. That is to say, there was a difference of opinion between the officers of the government who drafted the circular and the courts as to the support that there was in the law for the terms of the circular. The government forthwith passed another order in council on the 15th of March, 1910, which unquestionably brought the law actually in accord with the terms of the circular of June 4, 1909. In order that there might be no question as to the ampleness of the notice, care was taken that the substantial terms of the circular of June 4, 1909, should not be varied by order in council of the 15th of March, 1910. I submit, therefore,, that so long as parliament places on the statute-book a law providing for -the selection and restriction of immigration, the government is bound to carry that policy out, and I -submit further, that the government has given all reasonable notice as to the terms of the law that is being enforced and the necessity for a money qualification.
I have no fault to find with a restrictive or selective law; my point is that in all fairness to these people a test should be made on the other side and not when they land here.

speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege and I think to some extent my duty to try and meet the wishes of my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty), I will not press the Bill to-day. I will try and arrange with m.y hon. friend on the other side as to when it can be taken up.
Motion withdrawn.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution.
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Civil Service Act by providing for the appointment of temporary clerks for the compilation of any decennial census, who may be employed for a period not exceeding tliree years, and who shall be eligible for the annual statutory increases provided by the Civil Service Amendment Act, 1908; by providing that the salary of a temporary clerk employed under section 23 of the said Act shall not be greater than the minimum salary authorized for subdivision B of the second division, subject to be increased as authorized by section 33 of the said Act; and for the payment to collectors of customs of a salary not greater than $4,500 per annum: and for the payment of officers of inland revenue salaries not greater than the following maximum, viz.; inspectors, $3,200:	collectors, $2,800; deputy collectors, $2,200; accountants, $1,800 ; special class excisemen, $2,500; first, second and third class excisemen, $1,500; probationary excisemen, $600; stenographers and typewriters, $700 ; messengers, $800; and for the payment of officers of the Post Office Department, as follows, viz.; post office inspectors on appointment, $2,500, with an annual increase to a maximum of $3,500; assistant post office inspectors and superintendents of the railway mail service on appointment. $1,600, with an annual increase to a maximum of $2,500, and to author-

ize the increase to the minimum of the salary of any such officers whose salary is at present less than the minimum; and assistant postmasters, on appointment, a salary of not less than $1,100 and not more than $2,800, and that the said salaries and increases shall be payable as from the first day of April, 1910.
Is it the intention of the minister to appoint more than one Census Commissioner?

This resolution refers only to the appointment of extra clerks required for_ compiling the census returns in Ottawa. Under the present Act temporary clerks can only be employed for six months, and the census clerks will be required certainly for from two to three years. By this legislation we will be empowered to employ temporary clerks for a longer period than the Act provides.

There is a provision in the Census _ Act for the permanent taking of information in connection with the census; who is to be in charge of the whole of that new extra work in connection with the new general census?
The census commissioner.
Mr. Blue?
Yes.
Is it the intention of the minister to appoint some one to act jointly with Mr. Blue in supervising generally the census in all provinces?

No, we have the secretary of the Census Bureau and other chief officers. It is not my intention to appoint any chief officers for the general work. There will be census commissioners appointed in each province, but they will be outside and not in the inside service under the Civil Service Act.
There will be no joint commissioner with Mr. Blue?
No.

Is it not a fact that for the taking of the census of 1900 there was a joint commissioner with Mr. Blue? I refer to Mr. Cote.
_ Mr. FISHER. No, Mr. Cote was the assistant and occupied the same position with relation to Mr. Blue that Mr. St. Denis does.
There will be no assistant to Mr. Blue for the next census?
None outside the present secretary of the office in the department- Mr. St. Denis.
Will Mr. St. Denis have the same powers as Mr. Blue?
No.

There will be no supervision or control at all beyond that of Mr. Blue?
Mr. FISHER, Certainly not.
I understood Mr. Cote had equal power with Mr. Blue.
No, my hon. friend is entirely misinformed. Mr. Blue, had absolute power and control of the whole census, and Mr. Cote was one of his assistant officers. .

I notice that provision is made that these clerks are to be allowed a salary not greater than the minimum salary authorized for subdivision B of the second division. That is in reference to clerks employed to compile the census?
Yes.
They are to be appointed as ordinary temporary clerks commencing at $500 just like temporary clerks do now.

The only difference is that we will be entitled to employ them for a longer period than we are now authorized to appoint temporary clerks for, and being employed for perhaps two or three years, they will be entitled to statutory increases, the same as permanent clerks will be during the period of their employment.
That is an increase of $50?
Yes.
Then they come in at $500?

Under this Act we are arranging that some temporary clerks may be employed in subdivision B of the second division the same as in the third division, and it may be that a few of the temporary clerks for the census who will have charge of a block of other clerks will come in at a higher degree-that is at $800 instead of $500-at the minimum of the second division instead of the minimum of the third division.

Then you have not provided for that in your resolution, because you say:
That it is expedient to amend the Civil Service Act by providing for the appointment of temporary clerks for the compilation of any decennial census, who may be employed for a period not exceeding three years, and who shall be eligible for the annual statutory increases provided by the Civil Service Amendment Act, 1908; by providing that the salary of a temporary clerk-

That applies to the whole Act, and not to census employees only. One clause of the Act of 1908 defines our

powers with regard to the census. Then the resolution says:
-by providing that the salary of a temporary clerk employed under section 23 of the said Act shall not be greater than the minimum salary authorized by subdivision ' B ' of the second division, subject to be increased as authorized by section 33 of the said Act.
Under the present Act all temporary clerks have to go into _ the third division, subdivision ' B '. This is a provision that certain temporary clerks employed for a short time may be brought into subdivision ' B ' of the second division, instead of subdivision 1B ' of the. third division. This has no reference.particularly to the census.
What is the salary that they are entitled to in subdivision ' B ' of the second class?
It begins at $800. .
You could employ the whole of these clerks that you take in at $800.

Yes, if I thought of doing such a thing, but I would not think of it. The Civil Service Commissioners have found that we have frequently had applications from ministers through their deputies for the temporary employment of men of a higher character for special work, and it has been found impossible to get these men at $500 a year. We have, therefore, made this provision in order that they may be brought in at the minimum of the second division instead of the minimum of the third division. The Act of 1908 provides that temporary clerks shall come in at the minimum salary, and that has been held to be the minimum salary of subdivision ' B ' at $500. As I explained to my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart), it ha3 been found difficult to get men of the desired class for temporary work, and we therefore propose to pay them the minimum salary of subdivision ' B ' of the second division instead of that of subdivision ' B' of the third division. That will be done only where the work is entitled to be so paid.
They start at $800, and go up to $1,600.

I am talking of temporary clerks only, and temporary clerks could only be employed, except in census work, for six months in the year with no statutory increase. If a man is employed temporarily he can only be employed for six months. He can be paid at the rate of either $500, or at the rate of $800.
Rut your resolution provides that the term is to be three years.
That is for the census people?
Yes, but they are employed as temporary clerks?
Yes.
And they commence at $800, and run up to $1,600?

A few of them who may be employed as superior clerks, and put into that division, instead of into the third division, would commence at $800, but they would only be employed for three years, and during those three years they could only increase at the rate of $50 per year, or up to $950. There is another provision later on in the resolution, which says that temporary clerks may also have the addition which is permitted under section 33 of the Act, in case the employment is of a character which is not sufficiently paid for by the minimum salary of the class. For instance, if the Public Works Department required to employ an engineer for three months, under the present Act it could only pay him at the rate of $500 a year, and it would be impossible to get an engineer at that rate. We make provision that exceptional temporary clerks may be put into the second division, where the minimum is $800 a year. I do not propose to apply that generally to the census employees, whose work is in a class by itself, and is of a nature that would hardly justify such a provision, although I think that a few of them ought to be paid more than $500 a year. I may say that out of 200 or 300 census employees there would probably be not more than half-a-dozen who would be put in the second division.

I notice that the resolution provides for the payment to collectors of customs of a salary not exceeding $4,500. I have no doubt that in fixing this amount the hon. minister has given full consideration to all the circumstances that ought to determine the amount of the salary. I would like, however, to suggest that there are certain ports where collectors of customs handle a very large volume of business and a very large amount of revenue, and that there has been a very great increase in that business and that revenue since the salaries were fixed at the present amounts. Furthermore, in view of the great increase in the expense of living that has taken place since that time, the government might well take into consideration whether in such cases it should not pay even a larger salary than $4,500 a year. I have at present in my mind the Collector-ship of Customs of the port of Montreal. The immense increase in the business of that port and in the revenues collected there are matters of such public notoriety that it is not necessary for me to go into details in that regard. That immense increase involves a large increase in the work

imposed on the collector and a large increase in the responsibilities laid on his shoulders. Under these circumstances, I think I may be pardoned if I take it upon myself to urge upon the minister a further consideration of the question whether in a port of such importance the services of the collector should not be remunerated at a larger salary than $4,500 a year. When one considers the salaries paid to men in ordinary business life, whose responsibilities do not compare with those of the Collector of Customs of Montreal, it seems to me that the government might see its way to pay a larger salary. I make no reference to the qualifications of the gentleman who now occupies that position; T refer to the matter generally. If I did make reference to his qualifications, I am sure that the minister would agree with me that they would very materially strengthen the case which I am endeavouring to make, that as regards a port of such importance, at all events, the salary suggested can hardly be considered adequate or fair.

The matter which my hon. friend has brought up is one which is more for the Minister of Customs than for myself. The Civil Service Act, of which this Bill is an amendment, fixes the salaries of various officers outside of Ottawa. The Act as it stands limits the salary of collectors of customs to $4,000, and it is proposed to raise that to $4,500. The question as to whether a larger salary should be provided for collectors at such important ports as Montreal and Toronto is a question which I must refer to the Minister of Customs.

I am glad to find that provision is being made for an increase to the extent of $500; but I have felt it my [DOT]duty to point out the considerations which to my mind conclusively establish that the increase being made, while it is to be commended, does not adequately meet what justice requires in the case of the particular position to which I refer. The minister might at least have seen his way to adding the round $1,000 to the existing salary, and even then he would be very well within the mark.

I may oay that the reason I asked the Minister of Agriculture to change the schedule of the Civil Service Act which fixes the maximum salary of collectors of customs at $4,000 was that I might be able, with the consent of Council, to given an increase of salary to the collector in Montreal and perhaps also to the collector at Toronto. The hon. minister thinks we should make the amount $5,000 instead of $4,500. Increasing the maximum will not enable us to deal with any great number of collectors of customs, because we would not feel warranted in asking that 221
the salaries of many of them should exceed $4,000, except at Montreal and Toronto, and possibly Winnipeg. The business done at Winnipeg does not seem to warrant it, but the cost of living there seems to do so. There is difficulty, however, in this matter. The Collector of Customs at Montreal is certainly a good officer, and we value him; but in the days gone by we could not give him more than $4,000, because it seemed to be ratheT an anomaly that the deputy Minister of Customs at Ottawa, who is charged with the administration of the law all over-the Dominion, only got $4,000, and it seemed to me that an officer subordinate to him should not be given any more, perhaps not as much. But a year ago the House was considerate enough to advance the salaries of the deputies, so that the Commissioner of Customs now gets $5,000. That opened the way to removing the difficulty which I had experienced before. If we were to advance tne maximum salary of any collector of customs to $5,000, that would bring up the question of advancing the salary of the deputy, which I suppose would bring up the question of advancing the salaries of all the deputies, and we would be in the same position that we were in before. Of course, we have to proceed gradually in these matters and try to do justice. In another year there may have to be a further revision of salaries. Circumstances seem to point in that direction, as valuable officers require more than was paid in years gone by. Of course, we could not now change the amount in this resolution even if we desired to do so. Another resolution would have to be brought down. So, perhaps, we had better let this go, for the time being at any rate, and at another time something may be done in the direction of what my hon. friend desires.

I understand that the salary of the collector of customs in the city of Halifax has been at the same figure for upwards of 30 years. We have a man in that position who was taken from his business and appointed 4 or 5 years ago. He is a very competent officer, he enjoys the confidence of all classes of people in Halifax, and I am sure also he enjoys the confidence of the Customs Department, and we in Halifax think his salary should be increased. I need not press the matter further, because I have no doubt that the hon. minister knows the gentleman very well, and I hope he will see his way clear to increase his salary to at least $4,500.

The objection to this resolution is that it only deals with a fraction of the service. The minister has admitted over and over again that the salaries of various classes are low and ought to be raised. Therefore, in submitting a resolution to the House, I would

have expected that he would have included the whole service. In many cases we are increasing the salaries of the heads, but not those of the lower grades. If the increased cost of living entitles the higher officers to an increase, surely it ought to apply to those of the lower grades as well; yet they are not included in this list. When the government brings down a measure to deal with this question at all, it seems to me they should bring down one that would include the whole service entitled to an increase of salary.

I may say tha? in the old Civil Service Act there is a schedule which fixed certain salaries of the outside service in the Departments of Inland Eevenue, Customs and Post Office. In other departments of the outside service the ministers are free to increase the salaries of the officers as they see fit out of a lump vote. In this resolution the Minister of Inland Eevenue proposes a change, raising the whole schedule from the higher officers down to the very lowest.
What about the larger towns?

In the towns the postmasters are paid out of the revenue, while in the city offices they are paid out of appropriations. In the town post offices the postmaster, appoints his own staff, and we bring them under this scale when the postage collections and revnues are between |20,000 and $25,000, and the population is in the neighborhood! of 12,000, when we also give a free city delivery. These increases will affect 16 inspectors, 18 assistant inspectors, 8 railway mail superintendents, 7 assistant postmasters, and the amount involved will be $10,800 a year. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) referred to railway mail clerks. I stated the other day in the House that in my judgment the outside service, including not only the officials in the larger post offices, but the railway mail clerks as well, should come under the Civil Service Act. It is my intention during the recess to adjust their salaries, prepare a proper classification, and try to bring them under the Act which applies now to the inside service-in 1903 the railway mail clerks received an increase when Sir Wm. Mulock was Postmaster General, and I cannot, in justice to the other classes of employees in the outside service, discriminate in their favour. True, last year I increased the salaries of the lower classes, the stampers, the sorters and the labourers but there was no dissent to that proposition, and the general opinion was that their salaries should have been increased long before. In the higher classes it is a little more difficult and delicate, but I shall have to look into the matter, with a view of doing substantial justice to all. We are dealing with some of the higher officials this year, but it is much easier to discuss the salaries of a few whose efficiency is universally recognized, than to enter into all the intricacies of the other grades of the post office service. I believe that the increases proposed this year meet with the approval of the country.

The minister gives a very peculiar reason for not increasing the salaries of the middle classes this year. He told us he increased the salaries of the highest classes because they were the highest, and of the lowest because they were the lowest, but the middle classes he has not dealt with at all.

I am not prejudiced at all against the railway mail clerks; on the contrary I wish to do justice towards them. But they cannot sustain their claim against the ordinary clerks in the post office who have not had an increase and who do exactly the same work, and often under considerably more difficult circumstances.

Does not the minister think that their position and work are as 221 i
different from those of the man established in a permanent office as day is from night? They are subject to dangers, privations, hardships and extra expense that the man sitting in his office knows nothing about.

That is true in a way, but still there are good answers to all that. The railway mail clerk is meeting with dangers in the exercise of his functions, but on the other hand, he works only during some days of the week and he has days off. The clerks are closeted in the post offices, and they have to work day in and day out. Of course, they do not encounter the same dangers, but they have not the same facilities for breathing pure air as the railway mail clerks have. The railway mail clerks, it is true, are exposed to some dangers, but are not commercial travellers also exposed to dangers?
Not to the same extent at all.
They are on the same train.
The minister must admit that there is a wonderful difference with respect to the danger between the man who is in the hind car and the man who is in the car next the engine.

Yes, I admit that the railway mail clerk is not far from the engine, but, if the train runs well, if there is no accident, there is no more danger for him than for the commercial traveller in the first or second-class car or in the parlour car. I am not at all against the claims of the railway mail clerks. I simply say that I would not be inclined to discriminate between their case and that of the clerks in the offices. It requires a little investigation on my part, and I wish to be fair and just towards the different classes in the service. If I were to give an increase this year to the railway mail clerks I am sure that I would have a very strong protest from the clerks in the post offices. I must take the opportunity during recess of going into this matter. Time flies, and it should not take too much time. The railway mail clerks have already received a substantial increase, and they can afford to wait a few months more.
Would the Postmaster General tell us what was the increase that the railway mail clerks received in 1903?

The mail clerks in 1903 were granted a substantial increase in their salaries, and they were the only branch of the service dealt -with at that time. Up to 1903 the railway mail clerks were appointed in three divisions, known as the

first, second and third classes. Men in the third class were appointed at $480, alter two years going up to $520, after five years $560, and after ten years $640. In the second class they started aj; $600 and increased, after two years to $640, after five years to $720, and after ten years to $800. The first class started at $720, and increased, after two years, to $800, after five years to $880, and after ten years years to $960, and $960 was the highest salary to which any railway mail clerk could attain in addition to his mileage. It will then be seen that the increases in the railway mail clerks' salaries were at the rate of $40 for two years which is equivalent to $20 per year. It did not necessarily follow that when a man had reached the maximum of a class to which he belonged he would be promoted to the next class; in fact, in a great many instances he had to wait until there were vacancies in the other class before he could be advanced to a higher class. As a matter of fact he had sometimes to wait for two or three years before passing from one class to another. Owing to representations made with regard to their work, the dangers they ran. the hardships they suffered, and at the request of the railway mail clerks themselves, the different classes were abolished >'n 1903. Under the change made by Sir William Mulock a railway mail clerk is now appointed at a salary of $500 per annum, after six months probation, with mileage-my hon. friend knows what mileage is-and he goes on uninterruptedly, unless there is some report against him, by increases of $50 per year, until the maximum of $1,200 is reached. Under the old arrangement his maximum was $960. Since 1903 he has reached a very fair and substantial increase. His maximum is now $1,200 besides his mileage. Some Tailway mail clerks can make salaries reaching the very respectable figure of $1,900-not many, but some. This was a very considerable increase as the following figures will show. Under the old law a man starting at the minimum and going to the maximum salary of the first-class, $960, would attain that maximum in a period of seventeen years, but as above stated, where delays took place in promotion from one class to another until vacancies occurred these delays would probably double that time before he would receive the maximum salary.
Jfow, a man going on at $500 and receiving his increase year by year, "which will be granted to him if he is worthy, attains the maximum, not of $960 but of $1,200, in fourteen years as against seventeen years in the old days. The maximum has been increased by $240 and the time in which the maximum can be attained decreased by three years. Under the old Act if he had Mr. I.EMIEUX.
been granted his increase and promotion without delay, which was never known to occur, he would have earned in seventeen years $11,560, while under the new Act he earns $16,350. Under the old Act the first class railway mail clerk who had reached the maximum salary would have received $5,760 during his last six years, and during that same period under the new Act he would have received $6,740, or an increase of 17 per cent, which salary would continue year after year as long as he remains in the service. In 1903, when Sir William Mulock increased their salaries, the railway mail clerks were in a very inferior position and he placed them on a very much better footing. It is my desire and intention to still further improve their position, but it would not be just to the other classes of employees in the service who have no mileage allowance and who have not received any substantial increase in the past. During the recess I intend to bring about this reform, which I have contemplated for many years, and they will receive justice at my hands.

In an answer given by the Postmaster General to the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) the minister placed the stampers and sorters of the city post offices in the same class as the railway mail clerks. Are they required to pass the same examination as the railway mail clerks do?

Many of the railway mail clerks are appointed without the examination required by the Civil Service Act, but with the expansion of the postal service, especially in the west, it was found impossible to get railway mail clerks fully equipped, and so we take the best young men we can secure for the service, and after a period of probation they pass their examination and then come within the law. They have got to pass a more difficult examination than the ordinary stamper and sorter, but the clerks in the city post offices have to pass just as stiff an examination as the railway mail clerks.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

I am glad to find that the Postmaster General is providing by this Bill for increases in the salaries of some of the outside service, and also that it is his intention to take up during this year the other branches of the outside service. Last year I urged upon him that ,in the cities, particularly in cities like Halifax, where the mails come in at all hours, and men sometimes have to be on duty for eight or ten hours waiting for them to arrive, special consideration should be given. I tried also to impress

upon the Postmaster General that now that the Post Office Department is showing a large surplus, the minimum salary of a post office clerk in a city should be not less than $1,000 a year. Money is a great temptation to a man when he needs it, and occasionally we find some of the men in the post offices going astray. The increase of salaries has not gone far enough, and I hope the day is not far distant when no clerk will be employed in a city post office and expected to keep a family on less than $1,000 a year. Perhaps the maximum need not be much higher than that.
T hope and trust that the Postmaster General -will take this matter up during the year, and see his way to come to that conclusion. With regard to the letter-carriers-
They have had a substantial increase.

I am very much pleased with what the Postmaster General has done for them, but I hope the day is not far distant when a letter-carrier will not be asked to work for less than $800 a year. There are very few of the post office clerks who are not married. There is a rule in our banks that a clerk is not allowed to marry until his salary is $1,200 a year, and I think there should be a somewhat similar rule in our city post offices

I would like to be permitted to ask a question of the Postmaster General. Section 115 of the Postal Guide of 1909 reads:
All letters and other mailable matter despatched from Ottawa by the Speaker, or chief clerk of the Senate or of the House of Commons or the librarian of parliament, as well as all mail matter directed to the Senate, to the House of Commons or to the library of parliament, at Ottawa.
In the Postal Guide for 1910, the words,
' as well as all mail matter directed to tho Senate, to the House of Commons, or to the Library of Parliament, at Ottawa are omitted. May I ask under whose authority thi3 was done?

I have not fresh in my mind the order in council which dealt with that matter immediately after last session. As my hon. friend's question is not germane to the Bill, I would ask him to bring it up at another sitting of the House, and I will give him the information. At all events, I may say that nothing of the privileges of members has been barred by any order in council that has been passed.
It does not apply to members. I will bring it up at another time.
I w'ould like to ask the Postmaster General if stampers and sorters have to pass the same examination as railway mail clerks? [DOT]

Not the same examination ; but outside of the stampers and sorters there are in the post offices several classes of clerks who have as difficult and intricate work to perform mentally as the railway mail clerks, and who have as severe an examination to pass. I refer, for instance, to those in the Registry Branch, and those in the Inspector's Branch.
But these other clerks receive salaries going as high as $1,500 a year

The clerks of the different classes can pass from one class to another provided there is a vacancy. The railway mail clerks, when appointed after their probationary period, get $500, and they go up by regular annual increases to $1,200, and they get the mileage allowance besides. It is true that the mileage allowance is only intended as compensation for their living expenses on the road; but suppose you should offer a railway mail clerk employment in a post office at the same salary, without any mileage allowance, he would refuse. He regards his mileage allowance as an addition to his salary, and not merely as compensation to pay for his board. Let me give an instance. The other day a young man who is employed as railway mail clerk belonging tp the district of Montreal, asked to be transferred to the Inspector's Branch where there was a vacancy. He was quite competent. As railway mail clerk he had reached a salary of $600, if 1 mistake not, plus his mileage allowance. He was transferred to the Inspector's Branch where there is no mileage allowance, and since then he has been writing the department to get his mileage allowance, an;d says he never expected to lose it. I replied that in the Inspector's Branch there is no mileage, but that if he would return to his former position as mail clerk, he would get that allowance. I do not know what I may do as he is an efficient clerk. I may decide to increase his pay after a while, but he is not entitled to any increase just now.
In the case of a town where the postmaster receives from $1,300 to $1,500 per year, does he pay his own clerks out of that?

Yes.
