Mr, FISHER moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 205) to amend'the Civil Service Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill Tead the first time.
House again in committee on Bill (No. 103) to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act.-Mr. Pugsley.

Since this Bill was last before the committee, I have been endeavouring to see if I could not meet the suggestions thrown out by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker), and also my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), and two or three other hon. gentlemen opposite. I am going to propose that there should be added to the first section this clause:
The foregoing provisions of this section shall not apply to small wharfs, not costing more than $1,000, groynes, or other bank or beach protection works, which do not interfere with navigation.
* I think that will meet all the objections raised by hon. gentlemen opposite. If in practice it be found that there are still any objections to the Act, those can be met by amendment in the future. I am sure that the committee will realize that my only object is to keep control of the navigable waters in the public interest, and I would not authorize the chief engineer of my department to interfere with small wharfs or structures, such as my hon. friend from Halton referred to, unless they really and substantially interfered with navigation. The great object is to have a law under which people will recognize that if they are building substantial structures within navigable waters, they must first submit their plans to the department for approval.
The hon. minister might add boat-houses.	,
I have no objection.

I think that covers what my hon. friend from Halton spoke of, but I mentioned that in harbours there were occasionally rights of property where the title ran out into somewhat deep water and where a man might want to construct a wharf or elevator or something of that kind, and his building or structure would be actually in the water. I do not want to interfere at all with the passage of this Bill, the general object of which, I admit, is good. But what I ask is whether the hon. minister would see any objection to add the following as the last clause:
Nothing in this Act contained shall affect the right of any person to construct or maintain any structure upon his own property.
That is only to preserve the right of property, often very considerable property;. Where a man owns a right in a harbour, he owns the soil out under the water some distance. It is his property the same as the dry land. That man ought to be at liberty to build so far as his title goes, and Mr. FISHER.
yet 1 am not sure but that under the first clause of the Bill he might not be prevented by the government from building even on his own property. I would suggest the consideration of those words; if the hon. gentleman objects to them, I won't press them.

I would like to call attention to the condition of affairs at Port Arthur and Fort William that might be affected by the motion which the hon. member for Hamilton proposes. The water lots there run out two or three thousand feet. The indentations of the bay are deeper in some portions of the harbour than in others, and therefore' the lots are not all of equal distance from the shore line. Now, if the owner of those lots has the right to obstruct navigation on any of those lots the harbour -would close up. I had occasion to look into the matter a little -while ago, and I understand that the patents issued by the provincial authorities in later years all contain a reservation, they deed the property subject to the right of navigation, they are not to do anything on the property that would interfere with navigation. Formerly that precaution was not the practice. I understand that is the practice of the federal, government, the department issues patents embodying the same reservation. Now, in case of most of the structurds such as elevators and the larger wharfs, people are compelled to advertise in the papers their application to build, and frequently I have been called in by the board of trade or the city couneil, in both cities I may say, for the purpose of getting changes made in the proposed plan or location of these structures, in order that navigation may not be improperly interrupted. The amendment might work well in some places, but I would be a little afraid of it in these two cities.

I see an objection for the reasons which have been presented by my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) and also for other reasons which may be applicable to other localities. I have in mind my own province of New Brunswick. I think upon all the rivers of the province the old grants above the flow of the tide carry the ownership to the middle of the river, even on large rivers like the St. John. Therefore, if the clause were put in which my hon. friend suggests, the effect would be to remove from the department control over the erection of structures upon the navigable waters of those rivers. Then in the case of the foreshores in harbours which are owned by the federal government under the British North America Act, if the suggestion were carried out and a party should obtain from the Department of Marine and Fisheries a lease or grant of the foreshore, he might then go on in defiance of the Public Works Department and erect any

kind of structure upon that property, because under the law, even if he had a lease from the Marine Department, that would be his property. Of course, if he had a quit claim, which is sometimes given, it would be absolutely his property. While I would be glad to meet, if possible, the view of my hon. friend, I am afraid it would make the Bill inoperative in many respects.

At Gananoque, the Gananoque rivei; empties into the St. Lawrence about a quarter of a mile below the lower dam in the Gananoque river, and the owners of lots on either side of the river own to the centre of the channel, by virtue of a grant from the government to the founder of the village. If the amendment of my hon. friend from Hamilton was adopted, it might have the effect of destroying the navigation on that river. All our warehouses and factories are situated on either side of it, and vessels land their coal on docks built upon it. Under that amendment some person might be able to build structures out into the water which would destroy every factory in the town.

As I said, I will not press the objection if the minister doesn't wish to accept it. I know there are a great many cases where the property right is very valuable, but I would trust to the justice of the government to see that no mischief was done in such a case. With regard to other cases, such as Port Arthur, the patents provide that nothing should be done to restrict navigation. That is a common reservation in many of the patents, and this amount would not interfere with that at all. [DOT]

I have no desire to obstruct the passage of this Bill; no doubt there are many cases in which it may be desirable to have the authority which, under this Act, it is proposed to give the Department of Public Works and the Governor in Council. At the same time, I wish to draw attention to one fact with respect to the conditions of harbours on the Bay of Fundy. The hon. minister knows very well that there is a tremendous Tise and fall of the tide on that bay. I may tell him that so far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, there are a large number of settlements along the coast where grants of the foreshore or water lots have been made to the owners of the upland. Those grants extend out some hundreds of feet, but in many cases they do not extend out so far as the tide recedes. Consequently, at certain times these water lots, or the foreshore, are exposed. Now, in order to build a wharf on these foreshores, and some people do require facilities of that kind, they are compelled to expend more than a sum of $1,000. The sum of $1,000, as the minister knows, expended on a structure of that character on the shores of the Bay of Fundy, would be wasted, for the structure would not exist for a single year. Consequently, when he has placed the amount as low as $1,000, up to which it will be competent for persons to build a structure of that character without obtaining permission from the department, or without having the site of the structure approved by the Governor in Council, I must say that I think that will work a serious hardship to the owners of those foreshores. In the harbour at Digby, for instance, where the tide recedes many hundreds of feet, and beyond the point to which the foreshores are granted to the owners of the upland, wharfs are from time to time being built, costing from $3,000 to $6,000. Some improvements of that nature are contemplated there now, and this Act would interfere with them very seriously. I dare say that on rivers it is necessary that the Governor in Council should have that authority to determine on a site, but it would be a serious thing to have this clause 5 put into force, permitting the destruction of an unapproved wharf under the authority of the Governor in Council. If instead of $1,000 the limit could be made struction of an unapproved wharf in the open sea coast under the authority of the Governor in Council. If instead of $1,000 the limit could be made a higher amount it would be some advantage.
* Mr. PUGSLEY. This being a general law applicable to all navigable waters, it would not do to make an amendment which might be supposed to meet the case of one river, but which might cause very serious public inconvenience in respect to other rivers. The $1,000 was fixed to meet the case of hundreds of small structures erected largely upon the inland waters in regard to which it would be a hardship to require the submission of plans. But in the case to which my hon. friend refers, there would be no serious inconvenience or hardship, because if a wharf of a substantial, permanent character is being built to cost upwards of $1,000 there certainly would not be much inconvenience or hardship in submitting plans for the approval of the Department of Public Works. It is impossible to conceive. of a case where, if the proposed work would not seriously interfere with navigation. there would be any refusal to approve of it. My hon. friend will see that if we put the limit at $5,000 some one will say it should be six, or if we put it at six that we should put it at ten thousand. The main point to consider is whether the work is of a substantial and really valuable character.

I would think the amendment proposed would largely meet the case to which I drew attention a short time ago. Where possibly two or three or

four groynes would have to be constructed, sav by a county council, in a distance of 300 or 400 yards, would the value of $1,000 apply to each or would it refer to them altogether.	*
The $1,000 would not apply to a groyne of any kind.

I see that this only refers to bridges, dams, booms, etc., that interference with navigation, navigable waters are not mentioned. If I understand the new provision, it refers to piers, docks or other structures not included in the old Act. and if any of these cost more than $1,000 the plans have to be approved. I was wondering why the minister put it in that way. because if the work did not interfere with navigation what would be the object of any man with a $2,000 wharf, say on his water lot in Muskoka, coming to the department?

UndeT the present law there is no authority which is to decide whether a work interferes with navigation or not, and the only way that could be decided would be to go to law. For instance, when a wharf is built without the plans being brought to the department, if the department wished to take action the course would be for the Minister of Justice to be instructed to file an information for a mandatory injunction to compel the removal of the wharf. Then the question would have to be tried, and it would have to be determined whether or not, as a matter of fact, the wharf really interfered with navigation. My hon. friend can see how, as time went on, navigation would be interfered with very seriously, and how much better it is to have some disinterested, competent authority in the first place to determine as to these plans. When the matter first came before the House I mentioned the case of a bridge which was erected in New Brunswick. As the hon. gentleman from the city of St. John knovrs the Fredericton bridge was erected when Mr. Blair was the premier of the province, and although the river is navigable for steamers running between St. John and Fredericton and Fredericton and Woodstock, he did not think it was any part of his duty to come to the federal authorities. He said: We are going to put a draw in, we are not going to interfere with navigation, and because we are not going to interfere with navigation we will not submit our plans to the federal authorities. I mention that case, because it almost caused a crisis in provincial affairs at the time, almost caused the resignation, or the dismissal, of the government, owing to certain action which was taken by the legislative council, and certain further action which was contemplated, I believe, by the governor of the day. It was a case in which the plans ought to have been submitted to the Department of Public Works, and the Mr. HENDERSON.
chief engineer ought to be the one to decide as to whether or not a structure of this kind in reality interferes with navigation. That is the whole object of the Act. It is to get a larger control over navigable waters.
I presume from the way this Act reads that it will necessitate an application to the Minister of Public Works whenever a wharf is built in any of the harbours as well as on any navigable stream?
Yes. .

Take the St. John river, for instance, which the minister has referred to as a navigable river; no wharf of any size or kind can be built in that river after this Act passes until a plan thereof has been sent to the Minister of Public Works and has been approved by him.

Yes, but let me say to my hon. friend that to-day any structure of the kind is absolutely Illegal, and any man coming along with a motor boat, or steamboat who finds a wharf in his way in a navigable water can apply for an injunction, and compel it to be removed or destroy it as being an obstruction or a public nuisance. As the hon. leader of the opposition said the other day this is really an enabling, and not a restrictive Act, and it gives authority to make that legal which to-day is absolutely illegal, because the law gives any person the right to travel on the public highway, which a navigable water is, without being obstructed by a wharf or any other structure placed there without lawful authority.

Would the hon. Minister of Public Works let me read the amendment again?
The aforegoing provision of this section shall not apply to small wharfs not costing more than' $1,000 groynes or other bank or beach-protection works or boat houses which do not interfere with navigation.
I am satisfied with the clause as it reads. It refers to groynes, and other protection works just the same as it does to small wharfs. It might be made a little plainer by putting in the word ' or ' after the wrord ' dollars/ but I do not think it is necessary in order to give it the meaning I should desire it to have. My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) suggests that word.
There is no objection to it.

Will the minister permit me once more to draw his attention to the request that I made before, and which I trust he has not forgotten? I think it is a hardship to the county council of Halton, and the municipality of Burlington to be compelled to pay for those groynes or wharfs
That is another question.
It is another question.
Better discuss it on the estimates.

I may not have an opportunity of repeating my request, and I do not want the minister to forget it. I am quite sure that if he asks his local engineer at Toronto to visit this erosion two and a half miles from Burlington he will get information which will warrant him in spending half of what is requisite to protect this shore and let the county council spend the other half. He has given me the assurance that the engineer will go to Burlington and examine the erosion there, and I trust he has not forgotten.

My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) having got his [DOT] or ' in, I trust I may be permitted to say a word to the minister as to the figure he has fixed in regard to the value of a wharf that may be built without authority from the Governor in Council. I would like to ask the minister if he cannot see his way, in view of the fact that it would cost more than $1,000 to erect any structure at all on the Bay of Fundy shoTe, to raise the amount to $3,000. I do not think it is an excessive sum, and if this Act passes as it is, it will be a very serious encroachment on private rights. There is no question as to the interference of navigation in the instance to which I refer.

What does my hon. friend mean by interference with private rights? Does he not know that under the British North America Act the control of navigation is absolutely and exclusively vested in this parliament? Does not my hon. friend know as a lawyer that if I own the land simply between high and low water where the tide ebbs and flows, I have no power without express legislative authority to build a wharf there? The public may not try to destroy it, but does not my hon. friend know that any man would be entitled to go and destroy that whaif because it is an interference with navigation?

I am very much obliged to the minister for explaining what is no doubt the law, and which I think everybody understands. If we did not understand it before, I presume we do now. But, there has been an Act on the statute-book relating to this subject, and the minister apparently does not think it goes far enough. He proposes to go beyond what that Act prescribed and he is going to compel persons desiring to construct any wharf or structure of that character on their own lands, to apply to his department and obtain permission before proceeding with the work. But, he has gone a little
farther than that. He says that in the case of a structure which is not going to cost more than $1,000, he is willing not to enforce the provisions of this new statute. Such works are excepted. I would ask him if he could not extend that and make the amount $3,000 instead of $1,000? He may not think that it is an encroachment on private rights, but if a man owns the foreshore and he cannot construct a wharf on it without obtaining permission from the department, I venture to say that if there is a petition sent in by some good friend of the minister's, that permission would not be immediately forthcoming. If a man cannot obtain permission I think it is an interference with private rights. It does not necessarily follow that he is going to interfere with navigation. I cannot imagine that any wharf that is going to be built for $3,000 on the coast will be an interference with navigation. On lakes and navigable streams a short or inexpensive wharf may prove an obstruction, but when it comes down to the salt water 1 do not think the same objection exists.

This does not give any person a right to erect a small wharf; it simply says that you need not go to the minister for permission, but your wharf if it is an obstruction is bkely to be removed by anybody who likes. Inis clause does not give any permission; it simply says that one need not go to the minister to approve of the plans for such a wharf.
That is it; if you choose to do it, you do it at your own risk.
The minister would oblige us very much now if he would give us a definition of what ' navigable waters are?
If I could do that I would be qualified for the highest judicial position in the country.

In my constituency there is a dam now in course of construction which has had the approval of the Governor in Council, but I do not know how far the approval went or whether the structure complies with, all the conditions. Would this Act have any relation to that structure?
This Act would not apply in that case because the work has already been approved under the existing law.	.

The amendment proposed by the minister meets a great many of the objections I urged against the Bill on a former occasion. But, in a great many cases sawmill men maintain booms round their mills which are to a certain extent in navigable water, the purpose of these being to retain the logs while they are being cut
. COMMONS
up. It appears to me that the Act would prohibit this practice in future.

No, They can apply to the department submitting a plan of their proposed dam, and they can get approval. v\ e have continual complaints from persons living along navigable waters as to the erection of booms, such as that mentioned by my hon. friend from Pembroke (Mr. G. White) the other day in reference to a dam constructed right in front of the village of Petawawa. Surely the department should have reasonable control over works of that kind just as well as over fractures placed in navigable waters. When they submit their plans, if it is found the work will not seriously interfere with navigation no chief engineer would refuse to recommend approval. We are doing that constantly in the case of boom companies.
, Mr- ARTHURS. There are no doubt cases where a boom erected across a stream would be an obstruction, but this can be easily guarded against under the terms of the present law. What I am referring to is the case of booms which are constantly being changed, which do not necessarily interfere with the navigation of a stream or lake and of which no plans could be submitted to the department.. It would be a great hardship if a man who wanted to erect a small boom around a mill had to send plans to Ottawa.
' Mr. EMMERSON. The man who puts the boom there now is the judge as against the rights of all other people and often he constructs his boom in his own selfish interest as against the interests of the public This Bill merely enables the department to protect the public interest and it does not infringe in any way upon private interests because if the public interests are not affected permission will be given. At present these things are done without authority and in violation of the law.

I understood the minister to say that this was an enabling Act, but section 4 prohibits bridges, booms, or dams being constructed in navigable waters so as to interfere with navigation. The Bill does not include these words at all, but merely refers to navigable water so that it enlarges the scope of the existing law.

Under the present law if a person should construct a work of that character without the permission of the department and if it interferes with navigation, any person who is obstructed on that part of the river can remove the obstruction or get an injunction in the court, and the man who erected it is liable to be indicted as creating a common nuisance. What I meant to say was that this Bill enables any one who desires to construct Mr. ARTHURS
a work of this kind to get the approval of the department and then it is made legal.
Would this Bill compel those who are erecting dams on navigable water for the development of power, to come to the Department of Public Works every time they desire to put in a damp
If it is in navigable waters, yes.

For instance, on the Winnipeg river, a lease may be granted by the Department of the Interior for the purpose of generating water-power, and that lease may grant explicit powers to the company m the furtherance of that development; would it be necessary under this Bill for the lessees to come to the Minister of Public Works and submit their plans for the development of that power?

Undoubtedly that would be so if the dam was to be constructed in navigable waters. But without this statute and without its terms being complied with, or without a compliance with the terms of the existing statute, no lessee could, under a license from the Minister of the Interior, construct a dam in a navigable water.
If it was an interference with navigation.
I judge that any dam in a navigable water would be an interference with navigation.
In every Bill that comes before any committee, in which we grant powers of that kind, we provide that such works shall be subject to the approval of the department.

Under the amendment, if a dock or wharf is to cost less than $1,000, will the person who constructs it still have to apply to the department? If he has not to apply to the department, is he protected, so that no person can interfere with that piece of property, as could be done under the present law?

If it is a wharf costing less than $1,000, the Public Works Department cannot interfere with it, and the owner need not come to the department for permission to build it; but if he does not, he builds the wharf at his own risk, just as he does under the present law.
Would the minister consider favourably an amendment which would make this $1,000 apply to navigable streams, and say $3,000 apply to coast waters?
I could not do that.

In floating logs down the river it is customary to put around them a boom in order to tow them through a lake or a long stretch of the river, or to

guide them to the entrance of a channel where there is a rapid. If a person who owned a small bogt insisted on the right to pass through that boom or to remove it on the plea that the river was navigable, it seems to me that under this law he would have power to do so. Lumbermen have as much right to navigate these streams by towing logs down as any one else, and it is absolutely necessary that the boom should move along with the logs.
'Mr. PUGSLEY. That is a movable boom, used to float logs and to keep them together, and I do not think that any minister would hold that the section applied to that.
I do not know what any minister would hold, but I want to know if that is the law as laid down by the minister?
The owner of the raft of logs is exercising his right to navigate the river.
At the entrance to rapids he may stretch the boom and use it for two or three days, and may obstruct a navigable river in doing so.

There is another side to that question. In some cases rivers are unnecessarily blocked, but any lumberman who is at all reasonable would so arrange his boom as to stretch a long chain towards the shore so that any small boat or steam launch could get through. People work out such problems without much difficulty under the existing law.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 5,
I wish to ask the minister if this Act relates to an extension of with the repair of an existing structure?
It would, of course, extend to a new part, but not to any existing work.
It would not interfere with the repair of an existing structure?
No.
Would it not interfere with repairs if the party did not get the consent of the minister? Would it not give the minister the power, if he though! proper, to remove it?
I would think not, unless it were extended out farther into the channel.	>-
I thought the Bill was intended to give the minister jurisdiction over some works which are at present ih existence and which are nuisances?

No, it is only for the future.
Bill reported with amendments, and amendments agreed to.

AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide, in the case of escheats to the Crown, that out of any property so devolving the Governor in Council shall have power to make such grants as seem right;
(a)	To any person having a legal or moral claim upon the previous owner or a just or natural right or claim to succeed to his property.
(b)	To carry into effect any disposition of such property which the previous owners may appear to have intended.
(c)	To reward any person making discovery of such property to the Crown.
What is the object of the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have no general Dominion statute at the present time authorizing the disposition of money which may be received in the form of an escheat.
The word 'escheat', I might remind hon. gentlemen, primarily, perhaps literally, applies only to real estate. But using the word as including, not only real estate, but also personal property, which may devolve upon the Crown for want of any legal heir to a deceased person, we have at present in the consolidated funds of the country a sum of about $50,000 which has been realized and paid into the Receiver General as the proceeds of the sale of the estate of a man who died without having disposed of all his property by will. We have no authority to do anything with that money by any statute law. This possibly is the first occasion in which the necessity for some statutory provision on this subject has arisen since confederation because escheats, as every one knows, go to the provinces. This particular property, however, came from the territories before the new provinces were established there, and it may be that, in view of the provisions of fhe constitutional Acts of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, by which the Crown lands remain ithe property of the Dominion, all escheats from those provinces possibly might- follow a like destination. But, however that may be, and without adverting to that question of the future, so far as the territories are concerned, they were not a province, and it is quite plain that any property there which was escheated to the Crown for lack of heirs would fall to the Dominion as being the only govern* ment to which it could go. Such a thing

may happen at any time in the Yukon or Northwest Territories. AVith regard to the future, therefore, as well as to the money in hand, what. I am proposing is that by legislation the Governor in Council should be empowered to pay out of such moneys such sums as may seem right, first to any one who had a legal ot moral claim on the previous owner or a just or natural claim to succeed to his property. There might, for instanace, be an illegitimate child or other relations of a character *which .would seem to make it right to dispose of some part of the property, at any rate, in that way. To do so at jjresent there is. no authority whatever. The second proposition is that the Crown might be empowered to carry into effect any disposition of such property which the previous owner might appear to have intended. He may have made a will, but have defectively executed it, or there might be other circumstances indicating a certain intention. Finally it is proposed to reward any person making a discovery of such property to the Crown. These provisions are analogous to provisions in like circumstances of provincial legislation. The necessity for them is now shown, and it is desired there should be a general statute applicable to all people and cases of a like character. When mention was made of the intention to put this notice on the order paper, the hon. member for St. James, Montreal (Mr. Gervais), took exception, xearing that the proposition might be regarded as an attempt to encroach upon the undoubted rights of the provinces in this regard. I have since had the benefit of a conversation with my hon. friend, and I think he is quite satisfied that at any rate I do not entertain any such intention; but any possibility of danger in that respect can be readily safeguarded by the wording of the Bill when introduced, so as to limit it distinctly to what I intend, namely, the devolution of property by escheat upon the Crown in right of fhe Dominion and the Dominion only.

I think that is a power which the Crown in the Dominion ought to have. If there are any escheats to it, it has as much right to make a disposition of such escheats at any province. But, what I rose particularly to ask is whether the hon. minister has in view any particular estate, because in my section of tlie country there is the estate of a party who died out in Alberta, and in which it was impossible for the Minister of Justice to act upon the principles that are carried out in the different provinces.
- refer to the estate of Mr. Montgomery who died up there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the very estate I have in mind.

I have always thought the law should go further and provide for taking over all sums-lying in banks, for which there is no claimant. Money is frequently deposited in banks and the owner dies, there are no heirs, and the money is not disposed of but remains in the bank. We passed a law years ago which provided that year by year the unclaimed balances in banks should be published, but did not make any provision for disposition of the money for which there were no claimants. I have always thought that such money should revert to the Crown. I have never seen good reason why any individual should retain it. This Bill should go further and give the Crown possession of property of that character just the same as a portion or the whole of an unclaimed estate.
The suggestion made bv the hon. gentleman is one which would more properly apply to the Bank Act than to the resolutions now introduced.

I do not see any reason why, when we are dealing with the subject of escheats, we should not cover the whole ground. Of course, we could make such a provision in the Banking Act, but we could do so just as well in the Bill about to be introduced.

Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the resolution, which was reported, read the second time, and agreed to.
Mr. AYLESWORTH moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 206) respecting Escheats.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

subtopic: SUPERIOR COURT JUDGES IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC.

speechtext:
House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to provide for the payment to four additional judges of the Superior Court in the province of Quebec, each $7,000 per annum, and to one additional judge of the Court of King's Bench in the province of Manitoba $6,000 per annum.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SUPERIOR COURT JUDGES IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC.
speechtext:
This resolution is introduced to satisfy the demands which, so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, have been very strongly pressed for now as long as three years. In the session of the provincial legislature of Quebec for 1907, a provision was made for creating three additional judgeships at Montreal and one at the city of Quebec, in the Superior Court of the province. That legisiu-

tion duly passed by the provincial legislature three years ago, has never yet been supplemented by the necessary legislation of this parliament to provide the salaries. I am free to admit that the delay in that regard has been felt as more or le3s of a grievance by the province of Quebec. It will be in mind that early in this session the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) placed a notice of motion on the subject before the House, which was debated to some extent, and which appears now upon the order paper among the Public Bills and Orders, the debate not haying been concluded. I said in the discussion of that resolution that the explanation of our delay in taking action which the hon. member for Jacques Cartier thought was rather reprehensible, was the hope which we had entertained that it might be possible by some reorganization of the judicial system of the province of Quebec, or by some better utilization of the present judges in that province, to avoid the necessity for increasing the number of judges. That hope on my part has, I am sorry to say, turned out one impossible of realization. I cannot pretend to sit in judgment upon the action of the Attorney General, and of the provincial legislature of Quebec in calling for these additonal judges as a necessity, yet I cannot lose sight of the fact that to provide an annual salary for all time of $7,000 is tantamount to increasing the fixed charges upon the Canadian revenue to the extent of about $200,000. Every additional Superior Court judge just means that increased expenditure to the Dominion. Yet where the needs of the public require this additional expenditure, the Attorney General of the province is the appropriate and best judge of the necessity which the provincial legislation demonstrates by its enactment. In the case of the four judges which are asked for from the province of Quebec I cannot doubt that the necessity really exists.
Then with regard to Manitoba, the amount of the salary, to begin with, is not quite so large, it is only $6,000. But the legislature of that province, during the session before the recent one, I think not more than fourteen months ago, determined that their needs required the addition of one judge to the number of judges of their Court of King's Bench. Recognizing, as I have said, the fact that the administration of justice in the province is in charge of the Attorney General and authorities of the province, and that they are the people best in position to know of this necessity, we have proposed by the resolution under consideration to meet the demands of the province of Manitoba in this respect as well.

subtopic: SUPERIOR COURT JUDGES IN THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC.
speechtext:
I am sorry to say that I cannot concur in the views just expressed by the Minister of Justice, for the reason that as we pay the money we have a right to see that we receive service for it. It is true that the administration of justice comes within the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities, but the payment of the judges lies in our authority. The payment of judges constitutes a great responsibility, and we have a right to be assured that there is an absolute necessity for it. The minister says that he was trying to make arrangements by. a readjustment of the duties of the existing judges which would obviate the necessity of appointing four new ones, Now, we have a right to hear what difficulties he met with in trying to make an arrangement of that kind. I may be wrong, but from what I hear it is not so much new judges that is required in the province of Quebec, as a readjustment of the duties of the judges they have there now. I wish to protest against the assumption of the Minister of Justice that because he has received a requisition from the provincial authorities asking for the salaries of four new judges, that he is therefore bound to accede to that request, until he has assured himself that it is not possible by a rearrangement of the judicial system in that province to meet	all the	requirements.	I	am
aware that the position taken by the Minister of Justice is that which has been taken by all preceding governments. Of course that is a matter entirely under the control of the provincial legislature, which has charge of the constitution and maintenance of the courts. speechtext: As regards a new arrangement which could be made in the province of Quebec resembling somewhat the one existing in Ontario, which province I believe has an advantage in this respect, my hon. friend is probably aware that some years ago the Hon. Mr. Thomas Chase Casgrain, formerly a member of this House and one of the leaders of the Bar, while Attorney General in the Taillon administration, proposed as a radical reform that the province of Quebec should adopt the same system as exists in Ontario, that is to say, you would have district magistrates having jurisdiction in criminal and civil matters up to a certain amount, and the judges of the Superior Court, properly speaking, having residence in Montreal or Quebec, as in Ontario they have their residence in Toronto, and proceeding to the administration of justice by a rotative system, by circuits. Mr. Casgrain was ahead of his time apparently, because although he then commanded quite a large majority in the legislature, although this was not a party question, he had to withdraw his measure after having explained it to the House and submitted it to the Bar. I think that at all events I can speak with respect to the district of Montreal, and in my view there is an absolute necessity for an increase in the number of judges in that district. If there were room for criticism-and I do not propose to say that there is-I would be inclined to think that it is rather in connection with the delay in making this provision than in the actual making of it, because the facts set forth by the hon. Postmaster General are certainly not at all exaggerated. There is an absolute need in the district of Montreal for an increase in the number of judges, and that need has existed now for some time, in fact, there is a condition there that amounts very nearly to what might be properly described as almost a denial of justice. While all this is quite true as the result of a condition which should be a subject of amelioration, not perhaps by the direct action of this government or this House, I cannot sympathize with the suggestion that the position should be taken in this particular instance, at all events, that this government or this House should refuse to pay because it is in accordance with the system as we have it. But I do think that there is a serious responsibility upon the provincial government for maintaining, or refraining from endeavouring to remedy the condition which does make so large a number of judges necessary for the province. I am not unaware that there will be difficulties to be encountered by that government in remedying that state of affairs, but I think it is possible that there may be a great deal to be said in favour of the contention that a more strenuous effort might have been made in the past, and I think it is to be hoped that a more strenuous effort will be made in the future to readjust the system, and to make it possible for the work to be done in that province without a further increase in the number of judges. I think too that something might be done in regard to the manner in which the business is handled apart from the readjustment of the districts themselves. I am glad to see that at the present session of the legislature of Quebec there has been introduced legislation, which, if the reports
I have seen are correct, would seem to tend in the direction of ameliorating the situation in that regard. But whatever may be said about the condition that exists in that province, it is a condition which does exist and unless further provision is made to meet the absolute wants of the administration of justice in the district of Montreal, at all events, you will have a state of affairs where people are practically, so great are the delays, refused justice. I am quite prepared to approve of the proposition which is now made. I approve of the motive which has led the Minister of Justice to act with some hesitation in the matter, and I am not disposed to criticise the proposition, but if there were room for criticism it seems that it must be rather of the delay in taking action than of the action itself. I think that the provision which is being made is an indispensable one and an absolute necessity.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to the province of Ontario, I cannot pretend to speak to-day with the authority which I think I might properly have asked any one to repose in what I said on such a subject as this a few years ago. I certainly, when I ceased active practice in the courts of Ontario, did not think there was any necessity for increasing the number of our Superior Court judges in the province. Only a few years ago the number of high court judges in Ontario was increased by three on the establishment of the exchequer division of the high court. I do not recall in what yearthe judges of that division were appointed, but it is within the knowledge of every one that there was no chief justice of that division

until 1905. That is not yet five years gone by, so that in the province of Ontario we hail, only a few years ago, the whole of the work of the high court done by the twelve judges of the three divisions of that court. Subsequently their number was increased from 12 to 15, and in these circumstances one would have thought it was doubtful if so soon there was urgent need of adding to the number. It has additionally to be borne in mind that at a comparative recent session of the legislature the jurisdiction of the county courts in Ontario was very greatly increased. I am not sure of the extent to which the utmost jurisdiction of the county court in civil cases goes at the present time, but I think it is not less than $1,000. The effect of that legislation necessarily must be greatly to reduce the work of the superior courts. Every practising lawyer knows how large a proportion of the actual litigation of the Superior Courts always was in respect to sums of less than $1,000. I am persuaded that there cannot, therefore, be as great an amount of work to be done by the Superior Court judges in Ontario as there was prior to that considerable increase in the jurisdiction in the county courts of the province. But, while these things are so, 1 saw in the newspapers a few months ago that the judges of the Superior Court had made representations to the Attorney General of the province that additional judges were needed, and if the newspaper statement be correct, three at least were asked for. I had the advantage, two or three months ago, of a personal discussion of the subject with the Attorney General of the province, and he told me that he intended introducing legislation during the session of the legislature which has recent-Iv ended to deal with this subject. Since then he has written to me on two or three occasions, and he sent me a copy of the Bill which he intended to introduce, providing, as he stated in his letter, for two additional judges. Except in that informal way, and by a letter from the Prime Minister of the province on the subject, I have no knowledge of what has been done by the provincial legislature in this regard. I might say that I have not had any copy of the Bill as it finally passed, but I understand that it was for the creation of two additional judgeships. That is what the Attorney General said to me was his intention. I have not had, nor has there come to the government in any way, any formal application in the matter or any formal notice of the passage of this Act. In the circumstances, and I must admit that relying very considerably upon my own personal judgment in the matter, I have thought that legislation by this parliament, so far as as the, province of Ontario is concerned, might well wait for another 12 months without any interest really being Mr. AYLESWORTH.

A few years ago we increased the salaries of the judges to what

I thought was a very considerable extent. 1 have always regarded it as unfair to make a comparison between what is paid to a judge and what eminent lawyers get because of their legal ability. There is no class in the community which gets* as many of the plums of life as the.legal profession. As solicitors for railway corporations, banking corporations, loan companies and industrial concerns, they are paid great salaries on account of their knowledge of law, enabling them to give their principals information as to how they can evade the law and extract very large and onerous returns from the people. It is said that we ought to pay higher salaries to make these men judges because they can earn more in the profession. I think that is radically wrong. There is no profession in the country that earns half the salaries which they do, and yet I am bound to believe that many men in professional life are as intelligent, as brainy, as industrious and as faithful as lawyers are. But they do not get the returns-why? Because they are not able to tell their principals how they may evade the law. That to my mind is no proper argument why you should increase the salaries of the judges. I believe that 90 per cent of the people of the country agree with what I sav, that in proportion to their ability the legal profession of this country get more positions to which large emoluments are attached than any other class of men in the community ; and it is almost adding insult to injury to put that forward as a reason why the salaries of the judges of this country should be increased.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide rliat the bounty of one and one-half cant per imperial gallon payable on crude petroleum ironi Canadian wells, or from shales or other substances mined in Canada, authorized by chanter 52 of the statutes of 190R, may be paid to the owner or occupier of the' soil through which it is mined or won, or to such other person interested or injuriously affected bv the mining operations or works, as the Governor in Council mav approve.-Mr. Graham.

The meaning of this is simply this. The Dominion government gives a bounty of li cents per imperial gallon on all crude petroleum to the producer thereof. A corporation known as the Can-222
ada Company obtained patents to a very-large portion of the territory in western Ontario now operated as oil fields. Up to 1872 there was nothing in the leases which the Canadian Company gave to the farmers reserving to the company the mineral rights. After 1872 the company, in its deeds to the farmers, reserved those rights. The result of that is that a man owning a farm in Essex or Kent, where the oil wells have been sunk or where it is proposed to sink oil wells, is very much handicapped. Cases have been brought to my notice where a man's entire crop would be practically spoiled by people to whom the Canada Company had leased the right to sink wells. They go over a man's property, tramp down his crop, knock down his fences, offer a mall pittance for the damage, and tell him to go to court. No matter what reservations are made as to the mineral rights, this is manifestly unfair to the ipan who is tilling the soil. This matter came up in the Ontario legislature a few years ago, when I was a member of that House, and was discussed thoroughly. The hon. gentleman who is now Provincial Secretary, has stated that on a farm valued at $5,000, the actions of the lessees of the mineral rights would do damage to the extent of possibly fifty per cent of that value. A case was brought to my attention the other day in which it was said that the lessees went on a man's property and asked him if he proposed to farm that this year. He said certainly he did.
' Then,' they said, ' you had better move to another farm, because we are going to fill this one with holes.' Any action we take will not interfere in any way with the contracts between the Canadian Land Company and the farmers; but parliament has seen fit, in its wisdom, to present a bounty to the producers of crude petroleum, and what we propose to do in this Act is to give the Minister of Trade and Commerce the right to apportion that bounty between the producer of the crude petroleum and the farmer whose land is damaged by the work of developing these oil welis. The injury done to the farm lands is part of the expense incurred in the development of the crude petroleum industry, and we think that on that ground we have every Tight to protect the farmers whose lands are thus injured. If it has the effect of making the lessees more careful so that he will avoid any unnecessary damage, the farmer would be thoroughly satisfied, but if the lessee should inflict a certain amount of damages, the Minister of Trade and Commerce will have the. power to apportion the amount of the bounty given in such a way that the farmer will be protected to a certain extent. With that explanation I wish to noint out that the amendment provides for the insertion in the Bill of certain

words, which will make the Act read as follows:

What form will your regulations take, because the principal objection to this resolution is that it will be entirely optional on the government to act on it or not. There would be no objection to some mechanical way by which the party injured would be entitled legally to compensation, but this is left to regulation at the option of the government.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce shall be charged with the administration of this' Act, and may, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, make such regulations as he deems necessary respecting the payment of the said bounties.

The hon. minister does not appreciate the point I make. Your regulations are for the purpose of applying to the lessee alone the one and a half cent per gallon, and you intend to take that from him and give it to the owner of the land which you say is damaged. In what form are the regulations by which that apportionment is to be made?

I see the point my hon. friend makes. I tried to work out a mechanical way by which the thing could be done. The Minister of Trade and Commerce tried to work that out, but we found it impossible to make it mechanical in the statute because the conditions are so varied. The object of the Bill is to protect the farmers against damages as well as give them compensation, and we found it impossible to devise a clause that would operate mechanically, and apply to all the conditions that might arise.

But if you do not
have your clause mechanical, do you not see the danger that might arise?

* I appreciate the situation, and we discussed that point thoroughly, but came back to the conclusion that this is the only practical way in which we could work the thing out. Otherwise there might be some deserving cases which would not come within a mechanical clause. Take where the mineral rights have not been retained by a company, the farmer gets by arrangement one-eighth of the oil, and the bounty. That would amount practically to $2 per barrel. I started on that basis, but found it would hardly do because these men, to whom we are paying the bounty, do not own the minerals as do the other men. I tried another basis, and came back to the conclusion that the only practical way was the one we have adopted.

There is another question. The lessee has acquired by lease the right to thi3 one and a half cent per gallon, he has the right to the distribution, the same as any other lessee, or owner of land throughout the country. You deprive him of his inherent right by giving the money to another person. What right have you to do that?
The lessee has no inherent right. We are making him a present of one and a half cent per gallon; it is our bounty, and we can cease that whenever we like.
Suppose he has a lease and has that provision.
He has a provision entitling him to whatever bounty the government gives.
The government have passed a law agreeing to give a bounty. In that lease it is provided that the bounty payable by the government will go to the lessee.
We can do as we like with the distribution of our own money.
Not by order in council.

I am getting an Act. He caii provide in his lease that the bounty which the government says shall go to the producer, shall go to this man; but if parliament says that the government has the right to reduce the amount payable to the producer and give a portion of it to some one else, the government can act on that authority.
Why deal differently in the case of a lessee who gets his land from a farmer, and the one who gets it from the Canada Company?

The Act will give the Trade and Commerce Department the power as set forth in these words:
The said bounty to be paid to the producer of the petroleum or the owner or occupier of the soil through which it is mined or won, or to such other person interested as the Governor in Council by regulation approves.
If he is injuriously affected under this Act, he will get a portion of the bounty.

Those leases are generally taken by oil well drillers. They lease a certain territory. In the lease it is provided that a certain proportion of the oil shall go to the owner of the land. Unfortunately in those leases in question, the mineral rights were retained by the Canada Company. The parties who purchased from the Canada Company are supposed to have known, under the ordinary rules of civil contract, that these minerals were reserved. How will it be possible to work out a proposition of the kind submitted to us? Here is John Smith who has 100 acres which he bought from the Canada Company, and which did not give him any mineral rights; and here is Thomas Jones, his neighbour, who purchased his land with the mineral rights. Why should Smith be in receipt of any bounty from the government more than Jones? Because the second owner was the owner of the land, he was also the owner of the mineral rights. In the case of the Canada Company's lands the owner of the surface was not the owner of the mineral rights. Now in what position is the man who holds the mineral rights? How does he differ in respect of his lease from the Canada Company? Why should not the money, instead of going to the lessee of this land, go to the owner of the mineral rights in all cases, irrespective of any leases, or surface rights? But you are making exception. You make an exception in this case that the owner of the surface rights shall get the bounty. Is not that the case? The owner of the surface rights, according to the minister, is to receive this bounty if that land was purchased from the Canada Company originally; but if the land was not purchased from the Canada Company, if it was purchased from somebody else, the owner of the surface does not get that bounty at all, it goes to the oil lease. The Bill is also wide, because it says that if any damage can be shown, the man who suffers the damage can get the bounty instead of the man who has the lease. Another question was raised with regard to present leases. This law will be to a large extent retroactive. A man has leased land from the Canada Company, and he has contracted with the Canada Company to give them, we will say, one barrel out of every eight on 2231
the understanding that any government bounty shall go to him. Now he goes to work and finds himself cut out from that bounty if he does not get the bounty he would only give one barrel in ten, possibly, for the lease. Now this Bill is legislating these men out of their civil rights, and I do not think it comes within the purview of this House to do so. It is quite true that you will give to one man a bounty, and not to another man, and I do not think that is fair legislation. I know there is a grievance, but if a man's land is damaged I think he has relief in the courts, and can get damages. In the province of Ontario, if you are the owner of the surface rights, and a mine is discovered, the pefson who has discovered that mine has a perfect right to mine it. If he goes on that land and destroys your property he has to pay for it. The province of Ontario will see that justice is done in that respect.
But I can see a little further in this legislation I can see possibly a little nigger moving in the wood pile. Possibly in cases where some damage is done the" minister will see that some good Liberal friend will get this bounty instead of a Conservative. I have an idea that something like that is drifting in the background. I know that the chairman of the patronage committee in that riding, if he has any land that he bought from the Canada Company, he would be getting the bounty instead of the man who is the actual producer, the man who has gone to the expense of exploiting and developing this land. Everybody knows Jhat this business is really a wildcat business. It is worse than horseracing. A man guts his money into a piece of land. Another man may come along and find a good well across the fence that shoots a thousand barrels a day, and fifty yards away from that he may sink 4 or 5 wells, and not get a gallon out of any one of them. I think this Bill is quite too far reaching, and this House should have nothing to do with it. I cannot see how it can be worked out. The minister says he has had difficulty himself, I can quite apprehend it. Another thing, will this Bill affect cases that are now before the courts? The Ontario government has stepped in to see that justice is done. Then again, what about the purchasers? Hundreds of purchasers have leased this land, and this government takes away from them the right to that bounty and hands it over to the men who own the surface rights, and who have not spent a dollar on it. I think this is a very serious question.

In case after case the farmer has asked the operator to show him the lease, and they inform me that they have never yet been able to see the lease given by the Canada Company to the operator. The Canada Company does not operate itself, it always gives the right to a second or third party,- and these leases are handed along from one concern to another.

It is the custom in our country that when a man buys a Canada Company lot, it is practically under lease, but he has the sole right to occupy, to own, and to use that lot. I would not think that the Canada Company, in addition to that, would give the lease to another person to go on and buy a portion of that lot during the time the first lease or provisional lease was in operation.

I agree with what the hon. gentleman says, that they should not be able to do it, but they do it nevertheless. The Canada Company on no occasion has operated for oil in any section of the counties of Kent or Essex, but they give the right to second or third parties to whom these leases are resold. I shall give one instance. A gentleman named Stevenson, in Tilbury, owned a Canada Company lot. An oil operator came to that man's farm and asked if he was going to farm the land that year. Mr. Stevenson said he was and the man said: If you intend to farm you will have to get some other land, because we are going to punch this land full of holes. He had cleared the farm, paid the taxes, done all the improvements and built up a good home for himself, when the time came when the Canada Company thought they could get something for the lease they turned it over to an operator and he proceeded to drill it. Farmers have had to sit up at night to protect their crops from the operators and having wells put down so as to ruin the crops about the time of harvest.
Can the lessee of mineral rights do this without indemnity to the other, owner of the soil?
They do it,
Does your lease permit them to do it? I understand a reservation of mineral rights, but where the power is exercised there is an indemnity.

The only indemnity paid by any operator to any lessee, of the Canada's Company's lots would be $25. One ~1'hon. gentleman says: Why can they not go to the courts? That is what the operators always offer to do. They say: If you are not satisfied with what we give go to the court. The hon. gentleman knows how little chance the average farmer has in going to court against an oil company.
I am with you, we will stick to the honest farmer.
I appreciate my hon. friend's assurance that he will stick to the farmer. There is no doubt a great hardship to many agriculturist's in this country.

The farmer buys land
from the Canada Company. Who controls the right to enter his farm and get the oil, the Canada Company?
That is the great^ question; whether they do that or no!, the operator takes that right of going on the land and operating for oil, damaging crops and fences and ruining farms.
Have they no shot guns up there?

The hon. gentleman has expressed exactly the position the farmers have taken. In some cases they have threatened the operators, but I am glad to say have not done any bodily harm so far. One gentleman asked whether this bounty was to be paid under this Act, as it would be to a farmer who owned both the land and the mineral rights. I do not think that is the intention of the Bill; as I understand the Bill it is to give to the owner of the surface rights a portion of the bounty for the oil that is developed or found under his land. A portion of that is to recoup him for the damage he sustains to his farm through their operating for oil. It seems quite reasonable and fair and I feel satisfied the members will assist in this matter, because there are 'many, both Conservatives and Liberals, who will be benefited by it. It is not a case, as the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) said, of some particular person having the patronage or having some one with a pull getting all the money, it is a case of giving people their just rights in this particular section, and I feel satisfied the farmers will be delighted if the government will give them some assistance or relief in the unfortunate predicament.
Under the existing conditions the district is practically at a standstill. Owing to the danger of injury by oil operators the farmers will not take any steps to improve their farms or their buildings. If this Bill becomes law it will place these men on the same footing as their more fortunate
neighbours who own both surface and mineral rights, and the interests of the community will be greatly advanced.

I do not propose to be misrepresented by the hon. member, I am not opposed to seeing justice done the farmers, the only thing I am opposed to is injustice being "done to any portion of the community.
Does the minister not think if he wishes to give relief to these people he should give relief directly, and insist in paying the damages in a case of this kind where lands are entered upon? The very first man to protest against the bounty going to the surface-owners in that case would be the gentleman who owned, the lease. The Canadian Company without a question retain all the mineral rights in their leases just as deeds in Ontario for many years contained a clause retaining the mineral rights, and in the north nearly all the free grant lands, especially in the eastern portion of the province, contain a clause retaining the mineral rights to the Crown as the deeds in the northern parts of the country retain the pine timber to the Crown. As a matter of fact, the man who owns the surface right never owned the mineral right at all. The complaint he can make is that it puts him to inconvenience and damage to have people drilling for oil on his place. In order to recompense him why should the government penalize the man who takes over the oil lease of that land? Bear in mind that it is not only thq oil drillers from the United States who are concerned, there are others; farmers buy oil leases from their neighbours. Companies have been formed all over that country, and have secured leases for which they have paid, and they are entitled to a portion of this bounty. I think that we should meet the situation fairly. We should not say that the man who has the oil lease shall be penalized and the bounty refused to him. I think that is only a fair proposition. I do not wish to injure the man owning the surface rights, or to penalize the man who owns the lease, and has possibly paid a large sum for it. There are many other cases in that section where owners of oil leases go on land where they have no right to the surface, destroy crops and punch holes, and the man who owns the surface right has just as much complaint as those who happen to have received lands from the Canada Company.

The argument put up by my hon. friend is exactly the argument put up by the Canada Company. Previous to 1872 their leases carried all the rights. After 1872 they inserted a clause in the leases retaining to themselves the mineral rights. What farmer knew that that clause was slipped into that lease? It might mean anything or it might mean

nothing. Half of them would not know what it meant anyway. They thought they were getting their land. Every man who has an old patent from the government thinks that he owns the land.
And he does.

That is true, but those people who got land from the Canada Company would not know that they were not getting the title to the w'hole property but to only part of it. That being the case, the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggests a practical thing. We cannot interfere with a contract, that is a matter for the province, but we are giving, for the production of crude petroleum, a certain amount of bounty which is a gift and we have a perfect right by legislation to say how this gift shall be distrir buted. If the lessees of the oil rights have abused the privileges which they have got under their leases, we have a perfect right to step in and make them, in the ordinary vernacular, sit up, in so far as we can. This is a Bill for that purpose. If they do not damage the farmer's property they will get all their bounty, but if they have been regardless of and do damage to the surface rights of the farmers they should not get all their bounty, and if they know that they are not going to get it they will be careful with respect to the amount of damage that they inflict. My hon. friend says:	Let them go to the court. That
sounds well, but it is not business as far as the farmer is concerned. He may go to the court this year and get judgment for his damages, but he will have to go to the court next year and the next year after ' that. It is a great crop for the lawyer, but a mighty poor thing for the farmer. We have it in our hands, in connection with the bounty on oil, to deal with the matter and to say to whom and in what proportion it shall go. It is a fair proposition for this parliament to say by statute to the men who operate these oil wells and are injuring the farmers by inflicting damages upon the owners of the surface rights that we shall take the right to give them a certain part of the bounty, or to withhold a part in order to help pay for the damages that they may inflict upon the farmers. That is all that we propose to do here, and I think it is an act of fairness. It may not make much difference in the distribution of the bounty, but it will make a big difference in the damage inflicted upon the farmers by the lessees.

I am very glad indeed that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) has taken this matter up. I noticed in the newspapers a few days ago-it is only lately that the matter has been brought to my attention- that such a difficulty existed in western

May I ask the minister if any provision will be made with respect to damage done to property where no oil is discovered? They may go in and destroy a man's property and discover no oil. What remedy will there be for the farmer under these circumstances?
That is hardly a thing that this House can deal with.	,
What would be the result in a case of that kind?
There would be no result under the Act.

The farmer would get
nothing?

That would be more for the local legislature to deal with than this parliament. Ojir powers are largely confined to dealing with our own bounty with respect to the production of oil. It is the only way we have to reach this question, it may not be very far reaching, but we will go as far as we think we can in this regard.

It appears to me that the minister does not fully appreciate the position. Let me instance a couple of cases.
I go into that county and buy from a farmer mineral rights. I go to the Canadian Company and buy from that company the mineral rights on a particular section of land. In case I buy from a farmer, I am sure of getting the full bounty. I have an equally honest and valid claim on the property that I bought from the Canadian Company, but I am liable to a reduction for the simple reason that I have bought it from the Canadian Company. The minister says that the government have the right to dispose of this bounty in any manner they like. The government has no right to dispose of the money of the people to meet any such exceptional case as this. The government has no right to institute discrimination and to say they will give to one what they will not give to another. They may have the power, I doubt even if they have, but if so, it is a power that has never been exercised by any other government. If I buy mineral land from this company, and another man buys mineral land from a farmer, why should the man who buys from the farmer be penalized and not the other? I may do three times the damage to the land I purchase from the farmer, but I get no compensation, whereas if I do any damage to the land I got from the Canada Company I get compensation. Of course, you cannot make a law to apply to all sales of that kind, because it would be a dangerous principle to introduce, and it would be very expensive, but if you do
it in one case, you certainly ought to do it in the other. As to oil being a mineral, I may tell my hon. friend from Halton that the courts have decided it is, and further than that, they have decided that gas is a mineral.
That is some stupid judge.	.

You cannot speak of the judges in that way, and the general opinion is that the judge was right in that case. At all events, exceptional legislation of this kind is always dangerous, and the ' form in which it is presented in this Bill is most objectionable.

1 want to put this case to the hon. gentleman. A man buys the mineral rights from a farmer who owns them, and the farmer gets full pay for everything; it is a deal direct by the farmer himself. Is there not a big difference between that case and a third party coming in and leasing the rights from another farmer, who does not get a cent? My hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) says that the legislation i3 peculiar, and I admit it is, but the condition is peculiar. You cannot make any comparison, except theoretically, between the farmer who owns the mineral rights on his land and who makes a sale of them for which he gets a quid pro quo, and the man who until lately thought he owned his own land who has his property taken and who receives no damages. It may be peculiar legislation, but I believe it is practical legislation, and if it has the effect of making the third party, who is the lessee under the Canada Company, more careful as to the damages he inflicts, it. will do a great deal of good, and notwithstanding that it may be peculiar legislation, if it effects a good purpose, I think it ought to be approved of.
